extracted.intended_audience: trial judges and litigators (and juries) in U.S. patent infringement/invalidity cases
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for evaluating patent invalidity defenses (e.g., prior public use, on-sale bar, printed publication, prior invention/patent, obviousness) and related factual/legal standards in U.S. patent litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Public Use
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent claim is invalid if the claimed invention was in public use anywhere in the world before the effective filing date. An invention was in public use if the claimed invention was accessible to the public or commercially exploited anywhere in the world. An invention is publicly used if it is used by the inventor or by a person who is not under any limitation, restriction, or obligation of secrecy to the inventor. The absence of affirmative steps to conceal the use of the invention is evidence of a public use. Secret use by a third party is not public unless members of the public or employees of the third party have access to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors relevant to determining whether a use was public include: the nature of the activity that occurred in public; public access to the use; confidentiality obligations imposed upon observers; commercial exploitation; and the circumstances surrounding any testing and experimentation. If pre-AIA §102(b) is at issue, give additional instruction about exceptions under §102(b) and (c) when relevant. Cases cited: Pfaff; Barry v. Medtronic; Clock Spring; others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial Exploitation (as Public Use)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is commercially exploited if it is used commercially, even if the specifics of the invention are kept secret. An inventor commercially exploits an invention by selling a product made using the invention or promoting a product embodying the invention, regardless of whether and when the public learns about the invention itself, and regardless of attempted secrecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial exploitation can qualify as a public use even if the inventor imposed confidentiality obligations; sale or promotion of products embodying the invention is relevant. This definition is provided as an elaboration within the public use analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ready for Patenting / Reduction to Practice
rubrics_metrics.description: To be a public use or subject to the on-sale bar, the invention must have been ready for patenting at the time of the alleged public use or sale. An invention is ready for patenting when (1) it is reduced to practice, or (2) the inventor has prepared drawings or other descriptions sufficient to enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to make or use the invention. An invention is reduced to practice when the inventor has (1) constructed an embodiment or performed a process within the scope of the patent claims, and (2) determined that it would work for its intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This readiness requirement is repeated across public use and on-sale analyses. Reduction to practice requires both construction/operation and a determination of operability. Cases cited: Cooper v. Goldfarb; Pfaff; others.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-Sale Bar
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if, before the cutoff date (AIA or pre-AIA as applicable), an embodiment of the claimed invention was both (1) the subject of a commercial sale or offer for sale (pre-AIA: in the United States), and (2) ready for patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commercial offer for sale exists if another party could make a binding contract by simply accepting the offer. An invention was subject to an offer for sale if embodied in an actual product that was commercially sold or offered for sale, even if done confidentially. It is not required that a sale was completed nor that the sale terms disclosed invention details. The 'ready for patenting' standard (see separate entry) also must be met. Practice note on AIA exceptions under §102(b) and (c) where appropriate. Cases cited: Pfaff; Helsinn; Medicines Co.; others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental Use Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain activities will not be treated as a prior public use or on-sale event if they were experimental. Activities are experimental if they are a legitimate effort to test claimed features of the invention or to determine if the invention will work for its intended purpose; so long as the primary purpose is experimentation, incidental public use or incidental profit does not negate the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only experimentation by or under the control of the inventor or assignee qualifies; experimentation by a third party for its own purposes does not. Experimentation must relate to claimed features and aim at technological improvement rather than commercial exploitation. Testing done primarily for marketing is not experimental. If defendant proves prior public use or sale by clear and convincing evidence, the plaintiff bears the burden to produce evidence that the purpose was experimental; if that evidence is strong enough, the jury may find no prior public use/sale. Cases: City of Elizabeth; Barry v. Medtronic; Polara; Allen Eng'g; LaBounty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed Publication
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if the invention was described in a printed publication before the applicable cutoff date. A printed publication is maintained in tangible form (e.g., printed pages, electronic files, microfilm, photographs, Internet publication, photocopies) and must have been sufficiently accessible to persons interested in the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In determining accessibility, consider whether persons interested and ordinarily skilled in the subject matter, exercising reasonable diligence, could locate it; it need not be available to every member of the public. Issued patents and published patent applications are printed publications as of their publication date. The disclosure must be enabling—complete enough to enable a POSITA to use the invention without undue experimentation, judged by what a POSITA would have known as of the cutoff date. Practice note: when accessibility is disputed, give supplemental instruction on public accessibility. Cases: Blue Calypso; Orion IP; In re Lister; others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Invention (Pre-AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if the invention was invented by another person in the United States before the patentee invented it (pre-AIA §102(a),(g)). The defendant must show by clear and convincing evidence that (1) the other person reduced to practice a product or method including all the claim features before the patentee, or (2) the other person was first to conceive and exercised reasonable diligence in later reducing the invention to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prior invention must have been sufficiently developed that one skilled in the art would have recognized it would work for its intended purpose. This defense may be negated if the prior invention was abandoned, suppressed, or concealed. If abandonment/suppression/concealment is alleged, instruct jury on those terms: active concealment or unreasonable delay in making the invention publicly known supports a finding of abandonment/suppression/concealment; reasonable efforts to bring to market during a delay weigh against that finding. Cases: Teva v. AstraZeneca; Rosco; Dow Chem.; Apotex; others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Patent (Pre-AIA and AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if the invention was disclosed in a patent (U.S. or foreign) before the relevant cutoff date (pre-AIA) or before the effective filing date (AIA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-AIA: the earlier patent must have been issued before the patentee's invention or more than one year before the U.S. application filing date, as applicable. Under AIA: the earlier patent/published patent document must have an effective filing date before the claimed invention's effective filing date. If factual issues exist about whether the disclosure resulted from the inventor or one who derived the subject matter from the inventor, or issues of common ownership/assignment, give additional instructions on §102(b)(1) (AIA) and related exceptions as needed. Cases and statutory cites provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior U.S. / Earlier-Filed Patent Application
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may be invalid if the invention was described in a published U.S. patent application or published international (PCT) patent application that designates the U.S. (pre-AIA or AIA provisions vary) that was effectively filed before the patentee's invention or before the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-AIA: prior published U.S. patent applications/patents filed by another before the invention date can anticipate. AIA: prior published patent documents/published PCT documents effectively filed before the effective filing date can be prior art. If questions exist whether the disclosure was obtained from the inventor or whether subject matter was commonly owned or under obligation to assign, instruct on §§102(b)(2) and (c) (AIA) and related exceptions. Provide effective filing date as determined under 35 U.S.C. §102(d) when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness — General (Graham Framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention is invalid as 'obvious' if it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art as of the Cutoff Date. Obviousness may be shown by one or more items of prior art. The analysis must avoid hindsight and not use the patent as a road map. The defendant must prove obviousness by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness is a mixed question of fact and law. The following four Graham factors must be evaluated (scope and content of prior art; differences between claimed invention and prior art; level of ordinary skill in the art; and secondary considerations/other considerations). Each factor must be evaluated for each claim alleged obvious, and may be analyzed in any order. Practice note on jury vs court roles and effect of PTO having had (or not had) material facts (Microsoft v. i4i guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness Factor 1: Scope and Content of the Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the scope and content of the prior art by considering the items of prior art received into evidence. A prior art reference may be considered if it discloses information designed to solve any problem or need addressed by the patent or if it has obvious uses beyond its main purpose that a POSITA would reasonably examine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You must decide whether the defendant proved by clear and convincing evidence that a specific reference is prior art. If the PTO did not have all material facts before it, that may affect the defendant’s burden and should be considered; a jury instruction on the effect of new evidence may be appropriate (Microsoft v. i4i). List prior art stipulated by parties where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness Factor 2: Differences Between Claimed Invention and Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze any relevant differences between the prior art and the claimed invention from the viewpoint of a POSITA as of the Cutoff Date. Determine the impact of differences on obviousness of the claimed invention as a whole, not just a portion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider inferences and creative steps a POSITA would have used. If combining known elements yields predictable results, that supports obviousness; unexpected/unpredictable results or teaching away favor nonobviousness. A claim is not proven obvious merely by showing each element was independently known. Consider whether a reason existed at the time to combine elements and whether there would have been a reasonable expectation of success. If inherency is asserted, tailor instructions on inherency to the admissible evidence (see separate inherency entry). Analyze separately for each claim. Cases: KSR; Graham; ParPharm; others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency in Obviousness Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Inherency may supply a claim element missing from explicit disclosure of a prior art reference only if that element is present in or is the natural result of the combination of elements explicitly disclosed by the prior art; inherency cannot be established by probabilities or possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inherent element must be the natural result flowing from the explicit disclosure. Unexpected properties may be nonobvious even if inherent. Use inherency in obviousness analysis only when properly raised and supported by evidence; tailor instructions accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness Factor 3: Level of Ordinary Skill in the Art
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine obviousness, ascertain the level of ordinary skill in the field of the invention as of the Cutoff Date. The POSITA is presumed to know all prior art reasonably relevant and is a person of ordinary creativity who can use common sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parties agreed on level of skill, state the agreement. Otherwise consider evidence such as: (1) level of education and experience of persons actively working in the field (including inventors); (2) types of problems encountered in the art and prior art solutions; and (3) sophistication of the technology and rapidity of innovation as of the Cutoff Date. Cases: KSR; Graham; Ruiz; Envtl. Designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness Factor 4: Secondary Considerations / Other Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider other factors that may indicate obviousness or nonobviousness (secondary considerations), which should be considered before deciding obviousness. No single factor is dispositive; evaluate the invention as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potential secondary considerations include: commercial success due to the merits of the claimed invention (not advertising or non-claimed features); long-felt but unsolved need addressed by the invention; failed attempts by others to solve the problem; copying of the claimed invention; unexpectedly superior results; praise or surprise expressed by others in the field (including defendant); acceptance of licenses because of the invention’s merits. Carefully assess admissibility and nexus between secondary consideration and the claimed invention; the patentee bears the burden of proving a sufficient nexus. Only include instructions on particular considerations that are supported by the admitted evidence.
